lines.text: Why do some atoms pull bonding electrons more strongly than others? A single named property lets us compare that pull.

Electronegativity is the power of an atom to attract electrons to itself. A higher Pauling electronegativity value indicates stronger attraction. The definition is about attraction of electrons, first ionisation energy instead concerns removing an electron from a gaseous atom. Prerequisite bridge, the positive nucleus attracts negatively charged electrons. In a bond, electronegativity compares this attraction, first ionisation energy concerns removing an electron from a gaseous atom.
This definition supplies the quantity used to explain Periodic Table trends and to compare two atoms when predicting bonding.

Electronegativity, power of an atom to attract electrons to itself. Higher Pauling value means stronger attraction for electrons. Attraction for bonding electrons is distinct from the energy needed to remove an electron from a gaseous atom.
Why would power to lose an electron fail as a definition of electronegativity?
Two atoms can pull electrons with different strengths. What features of the atoms explain the difference?

Three factors influence the electronegativities of elements. Greater nuclear charge strengthens attraction for electrons. Greater atomic radius puts electrons farther from the nucleus and weakens attraction. Greater shielding by inner shells and sub shells reduces the nuclear attraction felt by electrons farther out. Judge their combined effects rather than treating proton number alone as decisive. Prerequisite bridge, identify occupied shells and proton number before comparing atoms. Inner electrons screen nuclear attraction, an additional occupied principal shell increases distance and usually inner shell shielding.
These three factors explain why the trend across a period differs from the trend down a group.

Higher nuclear charge strengthens attraction. Larger atomic radius weakens attraction. More shielding by inner shells and sub shells weakens attraction. Compare nuclear charge, radius and inner shell shielding together, a larger proton number alone does not decide electronegativity.
If nuclear charge rises but radius and shielding also rise, why can electronegativity still fall?
The Periodic Table lets you predict which of two elements is likely to pull electrons more strongly.

Electronegativity generally increases across a period. Nuclear charge increases, atomic radius decreases, and inner shell shielding changes little because added electrons enter the same principal shell. The stronger attraction raises electronegativity. Electronegativity generally decreases down a group. New occupied shells increase atomic radius and shielding by inner shells, these effects outweigh the increase in nuclear charge, weakening attraction for electrons.
Use these trends to compare atoms, then use the supplied Pauling values when the question asks you to predict bonding.

Across a period, electronegativity increases, higher nuclear charge, smaller radius, little shielding change. Down a group, electronegativity decreases, larger radius and more inner shell shielding outweigh higher nuclear charge. The Mg to Al dip in first ionisation energy does not imply a dip in electronegativity.
Why does increasing nuclear charge down a group not make electronegativity increase?

Going down Group seventeen from fluorine to iodine, nuclear charge increases but electronegativity falls. Which statement best explains this? Nuclear charge falls down the group, so attraction for electrons is weaker. The rise in nuclear charge is outweighed by the larger atomic radius and greater inner shell shielding. Electrons in the same group are not attracted to the nucleus, so the trend has no cause. Shielding stays the same because new electrons enter the same shell, so only nuclear charge matters. B Each step down the group adds an occupied principal shell. The larger radius and greater inner shell shielding outweigh the higher nuclear charge, so attraction for bonding electrons weakens.
Given two Pauling values, you can make an evidence based prediction about whether a bond is ionic or covalent.

Calculate the electronegativity difference as the modulus of, chi ay minus chi B, end modulus from the given Pauling values. A small difference means both atoms attract electrons similarly, favouring sharing and a covalent bond. A large difference means strongly unequal attraction, favouring electron transfer and an ionic bond between oppositely charged ions. Compare differences when several bonds are offered, do not rely on an unstated exact threshold. The presence of covalent character in some ionic compounds is outside this assessment outcome. An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. Electron transfer forms ions, it is not itself the force holding them together. Compare both atoms and use supplied values without inventing a universal dividing value.
This method applies the electronegativity trends, but use actual values supplied in a question for the final comparison.

Calculate delta chi equals the modulus of, chi ay minus chi B, end modulus from given Pauling values. Small difference predicts covalent bonding through sharing. Large difference predicts ionic bonding through electron transfer. Use the magnitude of the difference between both supplied values, electron transfer forms ions and electrostatic attraction bonds them.
Why must you compare the two values rather than judge bond type from only one atom's value?

L I B R has the smallest electronegativity difference, lithium attracts more strongly than K, and bromine less strongly than F. K F is the tempting opposite extreme, with the largest difference.
Which type of bonding is never found in elements?
An element contains one type of atom, so ionic bonding between unlike ions is absent. Covalent and metallic bonding occur in elements, and van der Waals forces occur between their particles.

three point one Electronegativity and bonding.
In one breath.

Electronegativity tells you how powerfully an atom attracts electrons to itself. Its pattern across the Periodic Table helps you predict whether two elements will share electrons in a covalent bond or form ions with ionic bonding.
Key ideas.

Electronegativity is the power of an atom to attract electrons to itself. Pauling values express this as a relative scale, a higher value means stronger attraction. The definition concerns an atom's attraction for electrons. It is different from first ionisation energy, which concerns removing an electron from a gaseous atom.

Three factors control electronegativity. Nuclear charge is the positive charge of the nucleus, more protons strengthen the attraction for electrons. Atomic radius describes the size of the atom, a larger radius places electrons farther from the nucleus, reducing attraction. Shielding by electrons in inner shells and sub shells reduces the attraction felt by electrons farther out. These factors act together, so a greater nuclear charge alone does not guarantee greater electronegativity.

Across a period from left to right, electronegativity generally increases. Nuclear charge rises as proton number rises, while added electrons enter the same principal shell, so shielding by inner shells changes little. Atomic radius decreases, strengthening attraction. For example, chlorine is more electronegative than sodium in Period three.

Notice the uninterrupted rise from sodium to chlorine. Heights and slopes are schematic, not exact Pauling values, increasing nuclear charge and decreasing radius strengthen attraction while inner shell shielding changes little.

Down a group, electronegativity generally decreases. Each step adds an occupied principal shell, increasing atomic radius and inner shell shielding. Although nuclear charge also rises, greater distance and shielding outweigh its effect on the attraction of electrons. Thus fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine, and chlorine more electronegative than bromine.

The first ionisation energy dip from magnesium to aluminium reflects removal of a higher energy, more shielded three p electron rather than a three s electron. The P to S dip reflects repulsion between paired electrons in a three p orbital, making one easier to remove. These electron removal effects must not be transferred mechanically to a sketch of electronegativity.
Method.

Read the two Pauling electronegativity values supplied in the question. Calculate the electronegativity difference as the larger value minus the smaller value, delta chi equals the modulus of, chi ay minus chi B, end modulus. The difference cannot be negative.

Compare the attractions. A small difference means the atoms attract electrons similarly, favouring covalent bonding through sharing. A large difference means attraction is strongly unequal, favouring electron transfer and ionic bonding between oppositely charged ions.

When asked to compare two candidate bonds, calculate both differences and choose the larger one as more likely ionic. Use the values supplied, do not impose an exact universal cut off unless the question gives one. The presence of covalent character in an ionic compound is outside this syllabus outcome.
Worked example.

Sodium has Pauling electronegativity zero point nine and chlorine three point two. Predict the bond type. Calculate the magnitude of the difference, delta chi equals the modulus of, three point two minus zero point nine, end modulus, equals two point three. This is a large difference, so electron transfer is favoured. Predict ionic bonding in sodium chloride.
Traps.

Trap, Calling electronegativity the ease of losing an electron. Why it's wrong, That confuses attraction with removal. Instead, State the precise definition, power of an atom to attract electrons to itself.
Trap, Saying shielding stays constant down a group. Why it's wrong, More inner shells are occupied. Instead, Explain both the increased radius and the increased shielding.
Trap, Deciding bond type from one element's value. Why it's wrong, Bond type depends on the difference between the two values. Instead, Subtract before predicting.
Exam technique.

For Define, use the exact definition. For Explain, name the factor, state how it changes, then link it to attraction for electrons. For Determine or Predict bonding, show the absolute difference, describe it as small or large relative to the alternatives, and give the bond type. Do not use ionisation energy exceptions to claim the electronegativity trend has identical dips.
